title: Qualcomm announces Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 for AI ‘hearables,’ even ones with cameras
snippet: Qualcomm announced the Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 as a substantial chipset for upcoming audio devices, with a massive focus on better AI performance for audio wearables. more…
fullText:
Qualcomm announced the Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 as a substantial chipset for upcoming audio devices, with a massive focus on better AI performance for audio wearables.

The Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 SoC is purpose-built for audio wearables, or “hearables” as Qualcomm puts it in its press release. With the push beyond simple audio performance, the chipmaker is taking the opportunity to build on what audio chipsets can do, as far as contextual image recognition for any camera-equipped earbuds the new chipset might be used in.

As for pure performance, Qualcomm notes the new Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 will be capable of up to 2x greater on-device AI performance. That comes at a lower power consumption rate by up to 40%. Translated to real-world use, the SoC is poised for AI wearables with local and online models that should require less frequent charges. Android XR devices would be a key example, since Gemini will need to live locally and gather information from real-world surroundings.

The chipset is also capable of Wi-Fi 6E, so OEMs can position devices to offer on-board or cloud-based AI access.

	

Qualcomm hasn’t abandoned the core principles of the audio chipsets. The Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 will have aptX and XPAN connectivity for better audio quality and Bluetooth range. But it will also leverage AI performance for better ANC built on Qualcomm’s 5th-generation protocol.

The chipmaker goes on to list a few theoretical devices the new SoC would be able to power. Some examples are traditional earbuds and headphones, as well as “open-ear hybrid audio designs, camera-enabled devices, audio glasses, and future multimodal wearables.”

Qualcomm doesn’t mention any key upcoming devices the Snapdragon Sound Elite Gen 2 SoC chipset would live in, but with Android XR devices and more coming from large companies, it likely won’t be long before the new silicon is undergoing real-world use.

title: Next year’s iPhone Pro models have ‘near-borderless’ design: report
snippet: Apple reportedly has a big redesign coming to next year’s iPhone Pro models, and a new ETNews report outlines what to expect from the “near-borderless” design and display. more…
fullText:
Apple reportedly has a big redesign coming to next year’s iPhone Pro models, and a new ETNews report outlines what to expect from the “near-borderless” design and display.

iPhone Pro 20th anniversary models to retain unique design, but lack certain display upgrades previously rumored

iPhone 18 Pro just arrived last week, and iPhone Duo will follow next month. But with Apple’s long lead times on iPhone development, it’s never too early for rumors about next year’s models.

We’ve long heard that Apple is preparing a unique design for its 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models next year. And today a new ETNews report offers the latest on what to expect.

Kim Yeong-ho writes that Apple “is still expected to move forward with a four-sided bending display” that’s “designed to create a near-borderless, full-screen appearance by curving the display around all four edges of the smartphone.”

So the defining characteristic of the 20th anniversary models seems very much on track, contrary to skepticism from Wall Street firm Jefferies last month.

ETNews does say, however, that two display technologies previously being considered for the new iPhone Pro models will not be implemented after all.

Apple is expected to postpone the adoption of two advanced display technologies—Color Filter on Encapsulation, or COE, and Low-Temperature Polycrystalline Oxide Plus, or LTPO+—that had been under consideration for its 20th-anniversary iPhone next year.

These technologies could have enabled, respectively, a thinner panel and greater power efficiency.

Industry sources reportedly attribute Apple’s decision to two main factors: higher memory pricing, which make it harder for Apple to absorb additional display costs, and the company seeking solutions that are better than current COE and LTPO+ options.

It doesn’t sound like either upgrade would have been especially substantial. What users will no doubt care more about is that the new “near-borderless” design is intact.

title: Adobe expands creative tool access to Google Gemini, brings Acrobat to Claude
snippet: Adobe today announced two major expansions to its AI chatbot integrations, bringing its creative tools to Google Gemini while adding Acrobat tools to Claude. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Adobe today announced two major expansions to its AI chatbot integrations, bringing its creative tools to Google Gemini while adding Acrobat tools to Claude. Here are the details.

Adobe expands tools to Gemini, adds Acrobat to Claude

For the past year or so, Adobe has been working to bring its creative tools to AI chatbots and other productivity tools, such as ChatGPT, Slack, and Copilot.

Today, the company is announcing two expansions to that effort.

First, Adobe is expanding its integration with Claude. The company already offered access to creative tools from Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, InDesign, Adobe Express, Adobe Stock, and more. Today, it is also adding Acrobat tools to the same plugin across Claude and Claude Code on desktop, the web, and mobile.

Adobe says users can get started as a guest, or sign in with their Adobe account “to unlock the full plugin experience, including higher usage limits, additional tools and continuity across sessions.”

Here’s how Adobe describes some of the new capabilities:

Work with Acrobat tools in Claude: The Adobe plugin now includes popular Acrobat tools for working with PDFs. Organize PDFs by deleting, combining or splitting pages; redact sensitive information; and convert or export PDFs to other file formats.

Edit and analyze PDFs directly: When you want more hands-on control, open your PDF in the new interactive editor to reorder pages, edit text or mark up the document with comments and highlights. You can also invoke the new Document Review skill and ask Claude to analyze your document and add recommendations and notations directly in the editor.

Refine designs with Express: Building on the conversational editing already available in Claude, you can now go further with a layer-based interactive editor for Express designs, giving you hands-on control over individual elements of the design. Select and customize images, copy, colors and fonts independently, so you can refine exactly what you want without needing to regenerate the entire design-all within your Claude workflow.

The second piece of news today comes for Google Gemini users across all plans. Starting today, Adobe is bringing tools from Photoshop, Lightroom, Adobe Express, and Firefly directly into Gemini.

This means that users can ask Gemini to enhance photos, create marketing assets, and customize designs using Adobe’s tools without leaving the conversation.

To get started, navigate to Personal Intelligence, select Adobe under Connected Apps, and sign in with your Adobe account or create one for free if you don’t already have one.

Adobe adds that users only need to describe what they want, and Adobe “orchestrates the right tools and steps to get you there.”

		
		

Some of the things Adobe says users can now do in Google Gemini include:

Create consistent, polished product photos: Upload your product photos and describe the look you’re after. Adobe can help optimize lighting and color, crop images consistently and prepare a polished collection that’s ready for your storefront, website or marketing materials.

Turn one design into content for your social channels: Ask Adobe to create social-ready versions while preserving your branding and messaging, making it easier to adapt and publish content wherever your audience spends time.

Customize professionally designed templates for your marketing needs: Describe your campaign, target audience and the style you’re looking for, and Adobe will surface Express designs that best match your needs. From there, you can ask Adobe to personalize the text, imagery and colors to quickly create polished marketing materials.

title: Anthropic to pay Akamai $11.6 billion over seven years in cloud deal
snippet: Anthropic has committed $11.6 billion over seven years to Akamai's cloud infrastructure, a bet on CPUs that could grow to about $20 billion, and in an unusual arrangement, Akamai is giving Anthropic a potential stake of up to 5% of its stock that grows as Anthropic spends more.
fullText:
Anthropic will spend $11.6 billion over seven years on Akamai’s cloud infrastructure, Akamai said Thursday. That’s more than six times the size of a $1.8 billion deal between the two companies that Bloomberg reported in May. The commitment isn’t ironclad; according to Akamai’s securities filing, it depends on Akamai meeting certain delivery and service-availability requirements, and either company can end the agreement under certain conditions.

The deal is the largest in Akamai’s history and continues Anthropic’s compute gobbling-streak. It also represents a bet on a less-hyped corner of AI infrastructure: CPUs. Demand for CPUs, the general-purpose chips that handle work like running code and browsing the web, has grown as AI agents take on more tasks, though Akamai didn’t say what Anthropic will use them for. 

Akamai won’t see revenue from the deal this year. On an investor call Thursday, executives said they expect $150 million to $300 million in 2027, starting in the second half, with revenue reaching an annual pace of about $1.7 billion by the end of 2028. 

To build out the capacity, Akamai expects to spend about $5.5 billion. It is also adding about $1.7 billion to this year’s capital spending to buy components such as memory in advance. 

As part of the deal, Akamai issued Anthropic a warrant, essentially the right to buy shares at a set price, for nonvoting preferred stock convertible into 7.7 million common shares, or up to about 5% of the company’s outstanding stock, at $111.33 a share. About 2% is expected to vest, or become available to Anthropic once it makes its first payment under the deal. The rest is tied to Anthropic spending more. Each additional $3 billion it commits to Akamai’s cloud services unlocks roughly another 1%, so the deal could grow by as much as $9 billion, to about $20 billion in total.

It’s the first time Akamai has attached a warrant to a cloud deal, and the contract is the largest in company history, Bloomberg reported.

The warrant flips the more common pattern in circular AI deals, in which suppliers — chipmakers and cloud providers — invest directly in the AI labs that buy their products. Here, the supplier is instead giving its customer a potential stake, one that grows as Anthropic’s spending with Akamai does. AMD used a similar structure with OpenAI last year, tying warrants to chip-purchase milestones. 

Anthropic is no stranger to such arrangements. Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and AMD have all invested or agreed to invest in the company while selling it chips or cloud capacity. CEO Dario Amodei told The New York Times last December that Anthropic does not participate in these deals at the “same scale as some other players.”

Akamai shares rose as much as 17% in after-hours trading on Thursday, The Wall Street Journal reported.

title: HomeKit Weekly: ULTRALOQ releases its first UWB smart lock that works with Apple Home
snippet: Hands-free smart lock unlocks/entry has always been a bit ahead, marketing-wise, compared to what the technology offers. Location-based auto-unlocks work until they fail for no specific reason, and using a key seems much easier. ULTRALOQ’s new Bolt Mission takes a different approach than most smart locks as its using ultra-wideband to detect when you are approaching the door, vs just tracking your location via GPS. more…
fullText:
Hands-free smart lock unlocks/entry has always been a bit ahead, marketing-wise, compared to what the technology offers. Location-based auto-unlocks work until they fail for no specific reason, and using a key seems much easier. ULTRALOQ’s new Bolt Mission takes a different approach than most smart locks as its using ultra-wideband to detect when you are approaching the door, vs just tracking your location via GPS.

HomeKit Weekly is a series focused on smart home accessories, automation tips and tricks, and everything to do with Apple’s smart home framework.

UWB vs Bluetooth

The Bolt Mission combines Bluetooth Low Energy discovery, UWB, and built-in radar-based presence sensing to figure out whether you’re actually approaching the door from outside or inside your home. That last part is what separates it from Bluetooth-based auto-unlock. The lock isn’t just tracking “Is an authorized iPhone near me?” It’s actually analyzing precise distance and direction of approach and making a local decision based on said data. The intent detection logic runs between your iPhone and the lock without requiring a cloud connection or a hub inside your home.

The end result is that you keep your iPhone in your pocket as the Xthings Home app runs in the background, and the door unlocks as you walk up to it. iPhone users who have used UWB features in AirTags will recognize how much more accurate this kind of spatial awareness is vs Bluetooth.

The rest of the new collection

On top of the Mission lock, ULTRALOQ is also launching the Bolt Pro and Latch 5 Pro alongside the Bolt Mission, and those two are worth looking at separately from the Bolt Mission. Both are Aliro-Certified, which means tap-to-unlock through Apple Wallet or Samsung Wallet. Aliro is the open standard developed by the Connectivity Standards Alliance, the same organization behind Matter, with support from Apple, Google, and Samsung. It’s tap-to-unlock from your wallet, but it’s not the same as Apple Home Key, which is Apple’s unique NFC implementation. Both are good, but they’re just different

If Home Key is on your requirements list, you’ll have to look elsewhere. If you want a tap-to-unlock option that works across platforms or you prefer the Aliro standard, the Bolt Pro is a deadbolt, and the Latch 5 Pro covers lever-style doors like side entrances, garage-entry doors, and home offices. Both support fingerprint, PIN, app control, and physical key backup alongside the digital wallet option. I have an older Bolt in my office, and I love the fingerprint unlock.

All three locks are Matter-certified and work with Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, and more.

Wrap up on ULTRALOQ Bolt Mission

The ULTRALOQ Bolt Mission is the lock I’m most curious to check out in this new collection. UWB-based detection is a ne  approach to hands-free unlocking, and if it works as described, it’ll fix the core problem that has made auto-unlock not 100% reliable for me. The Aliro-based Bolt Pro and Latch 5 Pro are solid additions to the lineup for anyone who wants tap-to-unlock across platforms, but just go in knowing they’re not using Home Key. 

You can buy the ULTRALOQ Bolt Mission and the rest of the new collection from Amazon or directly from ULTRALOQ.

title: As Android XR nears, smart glasses are only getting more popular despite Meta backlash
snippet: There’s been a near-constant stream of backlash against Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses in recent months, but that hasn’t stopped people from buying them, as a new report reveals that shipments have grown by over 250%. more…
fullText:
There’s been a near-constant stream of backlash against Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses in recent months, but that hasn’t stopped people from buying them, as a new report reveals that shipments have grown by over 250%.

Counterpoint Research reports that, in the first half of 2026, shipments of AI smart glasses have risen by 263% year-over-year. Meta holds 94% of the market with its Ray-Ban and self-branded glasses models, with Xiaomi and Alibaba each holding 1% in second and third place, respectively. 

Display-less glasses make up 96% of all shipments, with brands such as Rokid, Meta, Even Realities, and others splitting the remaining 4% of shipments for glasses that have a built-in display, but that segment is up nearly 450% year-over-year. Notably, no figures have been shared on just how many glasses units are being shipped/sold.

North America is the biggest market for display-less smart glasses, taking up 50% of the global market share, while China is a slightly bigger market for glasses with a display. 

	

Meanwhile, competition is brewing as Samsung & Google prepare to launch the first Android XR-powered smart glasses. The initial release will be display-less, focusing on integrations with Android and Gemini for interactions through your smartphone, Wear OS watch, and audio to accomplish tasks and interact with the glasses.

title: Google’s AI Wants to Call Stores for You — Here Are the Problems With That
snippet: Hate talking on the phone? Gemini’s got an answer, but you’ll still need to be in charge.
fullText:
Google on Thursday announced an expansion of its mobile Gemini AI capabilities, a new agentic feature built to handle everyday phone calls for you. Introverts of the world, rejoice — but also pay attention to the fine print, because there are limits to what Gemini can do for you.

This technology, which starts with a “@Call for me” prompt when using Gemini on your phone, is slowly rolling out to eligible users. Gemini could call a store to verify business hours or ask about product availability. With the right prompt, it could call a local restaurant and make a reservation for a specific time. Or it could ask about pricing for a specific service, such as dry cleaning a suit.

Gemini’s new feature is intentionally limited when it’s time to close the deal. It’s designed not to make any payments or share a credit card number, though it can share your name and contact information. 

			

More from CNET

That means, for many tasks you may want Gemini to handle, you’ll have to follow along with a transcript or listen in to the call, then use the “take over” option to sub in for the AI and provide sensitive data. This limits how much time the call-for-me feature can really save.

CNET Senior Editor and mobile expert Michael Sorrentino has questions about the new feature.

“While I’d like to test this out, the real measure of this feature will be both its transparency of being an AI assistant and whether businesses themselves will be willing to talk to it,” he told me. “I’ve long enjoyed Pixel’s other Call Screening features and Hold For Me (feature) for skipping hold music, so seeing Google get Gemini involved isn’t surprising.”

A representative from Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

You’ll need the latest Google phone for these capabilities.Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Will businesses play along?

Gemini will play an automated message to whoever takes your call, letting them know an AI is speaking, before launching into a conversation based on your prompt. But a lot depends on how the business responds.

Will there be a way for businesses to prioritize human calls over Gemini AI if they want to? What if a specific business location receives too many AI-generated calls and can’t reach human callers in a reasonable time? 

Google is restricting this feature from using emergency services, but many service-related companies could still run into issues. And it’s unclear how the new call-for-me feature will handle voicemail recordings or phone wait times, which are common in busy shops and restaurants.

When someone answers a call, questions arise about how employees will manage an AI interaction. The process remains distinct from speaking with a human, and unanticipated contact may cause confusion among staff. Organizations receiving a high volume of AI-generated calls will likely need to implement new operational guidelines to manage these interactions. While blocking Gemini calls is possible through an opt-out process, the availability of this feature for all companies isn’t clear. I also want to see how well the Gemini feature responds to a business that asks you to call back.

Finally, the calling feature has daily limits, though Google doesn’t specify how many calls you can make. This is probably to prevent overuse of Gemini’s energy-hungry features and to stop people from using it to make robocalls. 

How do I get the call-for-me ability?

You’ll have to jump through several hoops to use this Gemini feature if you’re interested. First, you’ll need to be over 18 and have a Pixel 11 or later phone. The service is only available in the US and in English for now. 

Next, you’ll need a Google AI subscription, which starts at $5 per month, and you’ll have to download the public beta of the Phone by Google app. Then you can update to the newest version of the Gemini app and use the @Call for me ability in a prompt.

Risks and issues

Google has set boundaries on the call feature, including restrictions about what sensitive data the AI can share. By design, it can’t provide data such as passwords or Social Security numbers. But that doesn’t mean it’s risk-free.

Google has confirmed that Gemini breached the security of three different companies this year without permission, raising questions about how easily the AI can slip past Google’s safeguards. 

We’ll be testing this feature as soon as we can and will report back.

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Tyler Lacoma
						

						

							Senior Editor / Home Security and Smart Home						
					

											

								

											Tyler has worked on, lived with and tested all types of smart home and security technology for over a dozen years, explaining the latest features, privacy tricks and top recommendations.
With degrees in business management, literature and technical writing, Tyler takes every opportunity to play with the latest AI technology, push smart devices to their limits and occasionally throw cameras off his roof, all to find the best devices to trust in your life. He always checks with the renters (and pets) in his life to see what smart products can work for everyone, in every living situation. 
Living in beautiful Bend, Oregon, gives Tyler plenty of opportunities to test the latest tech in every kind of weather and temperature. But when not at work, he can be found hiking the trails, trying out a new food recipe for his loved ones, keeping up on his favorite reading or gaming with good friends.

title: Gemini’s Live Avatar Puts a Face on Its AI Agent. It’s Freaking Me Out
snippet: Pretend you’re not talking to a lip-synching avatar.
fullText:
I’ve noticed a lot more businesses using AI agents to process customer support requests. But now it’s getting weird. 

Google’s Live Avatar feature is now available for those with Gemini Enterprise. This comes days after Google announced Gemini 3.8 Live and Gemini 3.8 Live Extended Thinking. 

What exactly is Live Avatar? It combines an interactive visual experience with a conversational AI agent to do things like filing insurance claims through a video chat — which was Google’s example in its announcement. Businesses or those with Google Enterprise can choose from a few avatars to put a face to an AI agent’s voice. 

			

More from CNET

Live Avatar seems pretty handy for businesses. It can create live video avatars with lip synching for conversational videos and process live audio, screen sharing and video feeds simultaneously. Live Avatar can run tools and API calls while continuing conversations with customers. But imagine a cartoon or realistic-looking avatar’s lips moving to match the bot’s voice to handle your request. Creepy. 

Live Avatar also aims to create more fluid dialogue with native speech-to-speech for “more natural interruption recovery without dropping conversation context or backend transactions.” 

Google didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on when it will be available to the general public or how it plans to safeguard the information the AI agent receives during video calls (like, in the insurance example, your address, name and live video when filing a claim). 

Google has a few safeguards in place to prevent misuse, like choosing from curated, prebuilt avatars. If you want to create a custom avatar, you’ll have to go through a verification process, Google’s announcement says. All audio and video are watermarked with SynthID to keep all AI content verifiable.

title: Apple has reportedly ‘postponed’ AI pendant product
snippet: Apple launched arguably its first AI wearables last week with Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, which are gaining new ‘Audio Intelligence’ features alongside Siri AI. But today a Bloomberg report says a different AI product—the rumored wearable pendant—has been put on hold. more…
fullText:
Apple launched arguably its first AI wearables last week with Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, which are gaining new ‘Audio Intelligence’ features alongside Siri AI. But today a Bloomberg report says a different AI product—the rumored wearable pendant—has been put on hold.

Apple’s AI wearable plans no longer include a pendant, at least for now

The AI era has sparked a lot of software innovations, but so far that hasn’t really translated into brand new categories of products.

There have been attempts, to be sure, such as the failed Humane Ai Pin. And Meta has had some success with its AI smart glasses, but that market is still fairly niche.

Rumors indicate Apple has several AI-centric wearables in the works. And last week it arguably shipped the first ones: Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.

But according to a report by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, the company has also been working on a wearable pendant equipped with a camera. For now though, it sounds like progress on that product has stalled.

Apple has also been working on an AI pendant with a camera, though that project has been postponed. The device was conceived as something users could wear as a necklace, attach to clothing or place elsewhere on the body, gathering visual data for processing by the new Siri AI assistant.

Gurman reported earlier this year that the pendant would “serve as an always-on camera for the [iPhone] that also includes a microphone for Siri input.”

Now it seems Apple has decided to put the project on hold. Instead, it is focused on infusing the Apple Watch with AI, alongside new AirPods with cameras and smart glasses coming in 2027.

It’s unknown how AI will factor in, but Gurman also says Apple is exploring a new health-focused wearable without a screen that could better compete with WHOOP.

fullText:
Apple @ Work is exclusively brought to you by Mosyle, the only Apple Unified Platform. Mosyle is the only solution that integrates in a single professional grade platform all the solutions necessary to seamlessly and automatically deploy, manage, and protect Apple devices at work. Over 45,000 organizations trust Mosyle to make millions of Apple devices work ready with no effort and at an affordable cost. Request your EXTENDED TRIAL today and understand why Mosyle is everything you need to work with Apple.

The SSO tax might be the most backward pricing model in enterprise software. Single sign-on should be required for sign-up, yet SaaS vendors routinely lock it behind their most expensive tiers. It should be the opposite. You should have to pay more not to have SSO. The result is entirely predictable: companies skip it, weak passwords fill the gap, and hackers thank everyone involved. I think there’s a real opportunity here for Apple, and it starts with an acquisition.

About Apple @ Work: Bradley Chambers has been an Apple IT admin since 2009. Through his experience deploying and managing firewalls, switches, a mobile device management system, enterprise grade WiFi, 1000s of Macs, and 1000s of iPads, Bradley will highlight ways in which Apple IT managers deploy Apple devices, build networks to support them, train users, share stories from the trenches of IT management, and ways Apple could improve its products for IT departments.

The SSO tax is a security problem with a pricing name

I covered this in my recent article on Dashlane’s Vault Enforcement: on average, 37% of enterprise SaaS apps are not managed via SSO, leaving a critical security gap, especially given that adoption of password management is still low, all things considered. That’s a third of the average company’s app surface protected by nothing more than a username and password. Some of that is legacy passwords and setup complexity, but a meaningful chunk is vendors charging a premium for the login method that actually keeps organizations safe. When SSO costs 2x or 3x as much as the base plan, SMB will often skip it

Everyone in the industry agrees this is broken. Nobody with enough leverage has been motivated to break it. Identity providers charge per user, SaaS vendors charge for integration, and the customer pays more for something that should be required. Imagine if MFA costs extra?

Clever already solved this for K-12

Here’s the thing: this problem has already been solved once, just not in the enterprise. Clever is the SSO and rostering platform used by a vast majority of K-12 schools. I’ve been a Clever admin multiple times in my career, and I absolutely love the service. Side note: Their support is among the best in the industry. I recently called them, and it felt like I was talking to someone up the road from me who knew exactly what my problem was and how to solve it. Seriously, shout-out to the Clever support team and to Clever leadership, who invest in it.

The model is the interesting part. Clever is free for schools and districts. Application vendors pay to be on the platform because the Clever app gallery is how they reach customers. That flips the SSO tax completely. Instead of the customer paying extra for secure login, the vendor pays for access to the customer, and secure login is simply how the platform works. Districts came to demand Clever support as part of any purchase, and vendors fell in line because losing deals was more expensive than integrating with Clever. I will not purchase a K-12 tool that doesn’t support Clever. 

Clever was acquired by Kahoot in 2021 and has continued to operate as its own platform since. 

Why Apple should buy it

Apple already has the pieces around the edges. Managed Apple Accounts, Apple Business, Apple School Manager, Platform SSO in macOS, and Sign in with Apple all exist today. What Apple doesn’t have is the connective tissue: a true identity brokerage layer that sits between organizations and the thousands of SaaS apps they use, with an economic model that makes SSO free for the customer.

Buying Clever gets Apple three things at once. First, a proven platform and team that has already executed this exact playbook at a massive scale in K-12. Second, an instant, dominant position in K-12 identity, a market where Apple is already fighting for device share against Chromebooks, and where owning the login layer would make Apple hardware even stickier (Google owns this today with Google Workspace). Third, and most interesting to me, a model it can extend upmarket: Apple-backed SSO that’s free for businesses, funded by vendor-side participation, and deeply integrated into macOS and iOS

Imagine “works with Apple SSO” becoming a requirement in enterprise procurement, the way Clever support became one in district purchasing. Customers demand it in the deal, vendors integrate because they have to for a deal, and the SSO tax is dead. You can take this even further with deep integration on the procurement side with direct ordering through Apple.

Wrap up

The SSO tax persists because no one with leverage has been motivated to kill it. Apple has the cash. Apple is in a dominant spot in the enterprise at the moment, and killing the SSO tax would be a clear way to drive enterprise services revenue, but not from the customer directly.

title: TechCrunch Disrupt 2026: Ricursive Intelligence’s Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini on when AI starts designing its own hardware
snippet: At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Ricursive Intelligence co-founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini will take the Disrupt Stage to discuss closing the loop between AI and chip development. Save up to $200 on your pass before today ends.
fullText:
AI needs increasingly powerful chips. But designing those chips is itself a slow, complex process. What happens when AI starts doing some of that work, too?

That’s the idea behind Ricursive Intelligence. The startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from the process, and improve the next design — potentially accelerating development of the hardware that powers increasingly capable AI.

Today, designing a chip can take two to three years. Recursive wants to reduce that cycle to a matter of weeks.

At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026, Ricursive Intelligence co-founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini will take the Disrupt Stage for “When AI Starts Designing Its Own Hardware.” They’ll discuss closing the loop between AI and chip development, building self-improving systems, and tackling one of the biggest bottlenecks in the race toward more powerful intelligence.

Image Credits:TechCrunch

Want to hear from the researchers working to change how AI hardware gets built? Today is the last day to save up to $200 on your Disrupt pass. Secure your ticket by 11:59 p.m. PT — and get a second pass for 50% off select ticket types.

What happens when AI designs the chips that power it?

Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini have already shown that AI can play a significant role in chip design. Before founding Ricursive Intelligence, the pair co-led AlphaChip at Google, an AI system that could generate chip layouts in hours rather than the much longer process required of human designers. Their work helped design multiple generations of Google’s Tensor Processing Units.

Ricursive Intelligence is taking that concept further, building AI tools to automate and accelerate chip design. Its system is intended to learn across different chips, so the experience of designing one can improve how it approaches the next.

That creates a potentially powerful loop: AI helps design better hardware, better hardware supports more powerful AI, and those systems can then help develop what comes next.

What could that feedback loop mean for the next generation of AI? Secure your Disrupt pass with up to $200 in savings and hear directly from the founders working to build it.

From AlphaChip to a $4 billion startup

Goldie and Mirhoseini also co-founded Google’s ML for Systems team. Both were early employees at Anthropic and senior staff research scientists at Google DeepMind.

Goldie, Ricursive’s founder and CEO, holds a PhD in computer science from Stanford and was named one of MIT Technology Review’s 35 Innovators Under 35. Mirhoseini, founder and CTO, is an assistant professor of computer science at Stanford and founder of its Scaling Intelligence Lab.

They launched Ricursive in late 2025, and investors moved quickly. Within four months, the company had raised $335 million at a $4 billion valuation, including a $300 million Series A. Nvidia is among its investors.

Ricursive wants AI to automate more of the complex chip-design process, from component placement through design verification, and learn across designs as it goes. By accelerating chip design, Goldie and Mirhoseini believe they can open the door to new chip architecture and ultimately more capable and efficient AI.

See where AI and hardware development could be heading next. Register for Disrupt to hear Goldie and Mirhoseini discuss the technology, bottlenecks, and self-improving systems behind Ricursive’s approach.

How fast can the AI-hardware loop move?

AI models have advanced rapidly, but the hardware underneath them operates on a different development cycle. Ricursive is betting that AI can help narrow that gap.

At Disrupt, Goldie and Mirhoseini bring the perspective of researchers who helped prove AI could design real-world chips and are now building a company around taking that idea further. For founders, investors, and technology leaders, it’s a chance to understand why the speed of chip development could play a major role in what AI can do next.

Their session is one of 200+ sessions across six industry stages, roundtables, and breakouts at Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 at Moscone West in San Francisco. More than 10,000 founders, investors, operators, and tech leaders are expected, along with 250+ speakers and 300+ exhibiting startups. The matchmaking, dealmaking, and networking at Disrupt create opportunities to connect with the founders, investors, and builders shaping what comes next.

title: Meta is launching ‘VR Glasses’ next year for $1,300
snippet: Alongside its new audio-only and Ray-Ban smart glasses, Meta today also unveiled new “VR Glasses” which take the experience of a Quest into a far slimmer form factor with an external processing puck. more…
fullText:
Alongside its new audio-only and Ray-Ban smart glasses, Meta today also unveiled new “VR Glasses” which take the experience of a Quest into a far slimmer form factor with an external processing puck.

Arriving in “Spring 2027,” Meta VR Glasses are a second attempt at a high-end VR experience from Meta following the failure of its Quest Pro headset. And this is definitely a more refined and focused effort.

Meta VR Glasses aren’t a headset directly, rather going for a far more compact form factor that puts 5K displays in front of your face and offloads all of the processing and battery components off to a puck. The glasses themselves weigh merely 100g, around 1/5 that of the Meta Quest 3 headset. 

The actual form factor is similar to XREAL’s upcoming Android XR-powered Aura glasses.

	

Meta VR Glasses support Dolby Vision and Dolby Atmos, as well as IMAX Enhanced content – Disney+ will support VR through expanded aspect ratio starting in November. ESPN will also be bringing 8K streaming starting with college football, and more will be coming through NBC Sports, the MLB, and more in the future. 

Controllers are not needed, Meta says, with hand gestures for general use and even the ability to put a virtual keyboard on the desk in front of you. 

It’s all powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Reality Elite chipset and Meta says to expect around 3 hours of battery life from the puck for media playback, with 45W fast charging to top it back off. 

Meta VR Glasses will be available next year at a price of $1,299.

title: Google Messages rolls out new swipe for timestamps & reply gesture
snippet: Following the long-press menu, Google Messages is widely rolling out new ways to access timestamps and direct replies. more…
fullText:
Following the long-press menu, Google Messages is widely rolling out new ways to access timestamps and direct replies.

Previously, you could tap on a message bubble to see the sent time, read receipts, and RCS lock icon. Meanwhile, swiping left would let you send a direct reply.

A redesign today changes all that. To see timestamps, you can now swipe left anywhere in a conversation. This also shows the RCS encryption status. Being able to see all times instead of having to tap the bubbles individually is an improvement.

To reply to a message, you now have to swipe right on the bubble. Some amount of precision is required. You can still tap the message to see the read receipts.

	

As of today, the most widely rolled out design appears to be the old two-circle look instead of the single version that has been in testing for ages. In fact, in a real show of inconsistency, the new design widely appears on an individual message’s Details page and might also show up on the homepage.

Google changing the swipe behavior is likely the biggest disruption today. When you tap on a message, Messages will briefly have the timestamps peek out as a hint about the new behavior.

We’re seeing this widely rolled out with version 20260910_03_RC02 of Google Messages.

title: macOS 27 Top Features: much more than just Siri AI [Video]
snippet: Although Apple’s revamped personal assistant is no doubt the headlining feature in macOS 27 Golden Gate, there are many other new features and refinements in this year’s update that don’t involve Siri AI. Read our post as I cherry-pick a few of my favorite new macOS 27 updates, and be sure to watch our video as I walk through them all. more…
fullText:
Although Apple’s revamped personal assistant is no doubt the headlining feature in macOS 27 Golden Gate, there are many other new features and refinements in this year’s update that don’t involve Siri AI. Read our post as I cherry-pick a few of my favorite new macOS 27 updates, and be sure to watch our video as I walk through them all.

App icon revamp

macOS 27 changes almost all of the built-in app icons in some way, with a few icons like Siri, Preview, and Chess undergoing complete redesigns. Other app icons, like Finder, Photos, and Reminders, also receive noticeable revamps, with a trend toward emphasizing the Liquid Glass design language. Few app icons were spared changes in macOS Golden Gate, but many of the updates are subtle.

If you watch my video below, you’ll see slider comparisons showing how each app icon looked in macOS Tahoe and how it now looks in macOS Golden Gate.

Some of the updates, like the Photos app, I’m a fan of. Other updates, like Finder, I’m not fully sold on. Let me know what you think about the app icon changes down below in the comments.

Video: macOS 27 Top Features and Changes

Subscribe to 9to5Mac on YouTube for more videos

Widespread HDR support

One of the coolest things about macOS 27 is its broad support for HDR across the OS’s visuals. Icons, toolbars, and other parts of the Liquid Glass design language gain support for additional dynamic range that users of HDR-capable displays will immediately notice.

To identify which elements have additional dynamic range, you can use macOS’ built-in Digital Color Meter utility to see where shadows or highlights clip while viewing native SDR values. Be sure to watch my video as I explore various areas of the OS to show HDR support.

Digital Color Meter: Compare the clipped area when viewing SDR vs brighter highlights when using EDR

If you’re a Studio Display XDR user, you’ve no doubt seen the differences, but even if you haven’t ponied up for Apple’s most expensive display, you’ll still be able to enjoy the benefits on a third-party display that supports HDR.

I recently went hands-on with Asus’ ProArt QD-OLED 32-inch 4K display, and, given the panel technology, the HDR effects throughout the OS stood out. Unlike Apple’s first-party displays with Extended Dynamic Range support, you’ll need to venture into Settings > Displays and enable the High Dynamic Range toggle to enjoy the benefits.

Most recently, I’ve started using the Dell UltraSharp U3226Q QD-OLED display, which I’m really enjoying, and I will be posting a review on it soon. On both displays, the HDR elements pop, such as the blinking cursor within the newly redesigned Spotlight/Siri AI interface.

Design updates

macOS Golden Gate features a ton of design updates to address complaints users raised about macOS Tahoe. One of my biggest complaints was the mismatched corner radii between certain windows.

macOS Tahoe’s egregious corner radius issue has been fixed in Golden Gate

Of course, this wasn’t the only complaint addressed, but it was the one that mattered most to me. Other areas that were fixed were the floating side bars, which are now back to being edge-to-edge side bars, toolbars have been revamped with an obvious line of demarcation, and the Liquid Glass effect itself has been improved, including a new slider that lets users have more choice over the amount of transparency vs tint throughout the OS.

Another major complaint from users about macOS Tahoe was the unnecessary clutter heaped onto the menus. In macOS Tahoe, nearly every menu option got its own corresponding glyph, which made the menus look like a mess.

Tahoe vs Golden Gate: Apple learned that not every menu option needs its own glyph

If every menu item has an icon, eventually you’re going to run out of icon options that make sense, while reducing the effectiveness of the glyphs that were there before. I’m so glad that Apple fixed this issue.

iPhone Mirroring

iPhone Mirroring on macOS 27 got three major improvements that make the feature so much better on Golden Gate.

You can now access Control Center from a mirrored iPhone.

You can resize the iPhone mirroring interface to match more closely the iPad mini aspect ratio.

You can play back DRM-protected content from your iPhone on your Mac without a blackout.

Needless to say, iPhone Mirroring just got a lot more useful in macOS 27!

9to5Mac’s Take

Although Siri AI takes up most of the headlines, macOS Golden Gate is not just about Siri. I cherry-picked a few of my favorite new additions in this post, but there are lots more to explore. Watch my full video for a rundown of everything new, and let me know what your favorite new features are in the comments.

Asus ProArt 5K Display – Pound for pound, the best external display for Mac

title: Google confirms Gemini hacked into three companies during cybersecurity test months ago
snippet: Following a Wall Street Journal investigation, Google has confirmed that Gemini went rogue in May 2026, accessing the internet and breaching the security of three different companies. more…
fullText:
Following a Wall Street Journal investigation, Google has confirmed that Gemini went rogue in May 2026, accessing the internet and breaching the security of three different companies.

As AI continues to advance in its capabilities, we’re running into more cases of models going rogue. Perhaps the most infamous has been from OpenAI in the Hugging Face hack, but there plenty of other examples, including from Anthropic’s Claude. These incidents, in part, have led to the public call to slow down AI development from Anthropic’s CEO.

But, behind the scenes, Google also ran into a similar problem. The Wall Street Journal reports, including a confirmation by Google, that Gemini was involved in hacking three external companies during a cybersecurity test through Irregular, an AI security company also involved in similar incidents that were previously disclosed by OpenAI, Meta, and Anthropic. 

The three hacks included one case of Gemini guessing a password until it gained access to the system, with the other two cases using credentials discovered in a public repository. 

	

Google didn’t disclose these incidents until the company was approached by The Wall Street Journal, citing that no harm was caused, and that the model stopped the behavior as soon as it realized it had breached the security of a real company rather than a simulated one. The report explains:

Google said that it didn’t consider the behavior an example of model misalignment because its safety measures helped it stop. It declined to share the name of the companies that were hacked, but said that all three companies had been notified.

In prior hacks from OpenAI and Anthropic, the models either didn’t realize the real company was indeed a real company, or simply continued in the hack in the latter’s case. 

Google’s Heather Adkins, VP of security engineering, said:

This event highlights the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.  In this case, the model acted appropriately.

It another statement to The Verge, Adkins expanded:

Our security team has a long track record of reporting issues we find in other people’s software and systems – even if it’s as simple as a weak password. We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes. These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.

The WSJ report further expands that, during the test in which Gemini went rogue, Irregular “unintentionally” left internet access open. Google also notified federal authorities when the hacks occurred. The exact Gemini model used in the test has not been confirmed, but the May 2026 timing alone rules out the latest Gemini models.

title: Apple vs. Adobe: How does iOS 27’s AI photo editing compare to Photoshop?
snippet: I’ve been using Photoshop’s generative AI features to remove unwanted objects and extend photos since Adobe introduced them in 2023. They’ve been hit or miss for me, but they’re certainly a lot faster than the old-fashioned approach of masking, cloning, and manually painting things out. But with iOS 27, Apple has significantly improved its Clean Up tool and introduced the new Extend tool, and I was curious to see how Apple’s offerings compare with Adobe’s. So, with the help of a friend, I put both to the test using a variety of photos to see how they stack up. more…
fullText:
I’ve been using Photoshop’s generative AI features to remove unwanted objects and extend photos since Adobe introduced them in 2023. They’ve been hit or miss for me, but they’re certainly a lot faster than the old-fashioned approach of masking, cloning, and manually painting things out. But with iOS 27, Apple has significantly improved its Clean Up tool and introduced the new Extend tool, and I was curious to see how Apple’s offerings compare with Adobe’s. So, with the help of a friend, I put both to the test using a variety of photos to see how they stack up.

For this article, my friend Jürg was kind enough to provide several photos from his travels throughout Switzerland and Europe. He takes much better photos than I ever could, and takes pictures of more exciting subjects than my corner of Ohio has to offer. You can see more of his photography on Instagram. I narrowed the selection down to six photos: three to test object removal and three to test image extension.

All photos were shot on an iPhone 17 Pro Max and edited on an iPhone 18 Pro Max running iOS 27.0. The Clean Up tool in iOS 27 has three options: Auto, Fast, and High Quality. I left the setting on Auto for all three tests.

Photoshop tests were done on a MacBook Pro running Adobe Photoshop 27.10.0 using the “Firefly Fill & Expand” model. I selected the objects using either the Object Selection Tool or Lasso Tool, then chose Generative Fill and left the prompt box blank.

For the Extend tool, I used whatever extension Photos selected by default. The Extend tool in Photos limits how far you can expand the edges of an image, while Photoshop doesn’t have the same restriction. To keep the comparison as consistent as possible, I used the result from Apple’s Photos as my reference, and had Photoshop create something in a similar size.

I made every effort to keep the HDR appearance as consistent as possible between the photos edited in Photos on iOS 27 and those edited in Photoshop, but there was some minor variation.

Making things disappear

Left: Original photo

Right: iOS 27 Clean Up

First up is the removal of this red chair in front of the yellow door. This was the first photo I tested with the new Clean Up tool, and I have to say, it left quite a positive impression. The result looks very believable, and the only real mistake I noticed is that the rivet behind the chair’s left armrest was also removed instead of being correctly reconstructed. It’s not something I’m convinced most people would notice, though, and it would be an easy fix to clone back in with Photoshop. I was particularly impressed by how the shadow beneath the chair was replaced with a texture that matches the surrounding scene while also maintaining the existing lighting.

Left: Original photo

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Photoshop doesn’t do as good a job as Apple’s Clean Up tool here. The chair’s shadow remains and looks more like an oil stain. The door’s rivets are misaligned, and one is obviously missing. The replacement texture also contains significantly more visual artifacts. Overall, it isn’t nearly as clean or realistic as what Clean Up produced.

Left: Original photo

Right: iOS 27 Clean Up

I was really impressed with Clean Up’s results here. Not only did it remove the plate with bread, but it also added a nice reflection of the mug and jars. Notice it even got the handle of the spoon right in the reflection. A nice detail. Clean Up also completely removed the plate’s shadow from the napkin. I thought removing a red plate from a red table of the same color might prove more of a challenge for Clean Up, but nope! If I had one nitpick, it’s that Clean Up left the crumbs from the plate, though removing them would be very easy to do by running Clean Up again over that area.

Left: Original photo

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Photoshop removed the plate with bread well enough, but again, it had issues with leaving behind an out-of-place shadow. The napkin looks dirty or wet here, but at least Photoshop didn’t leave behind as many pesky crumbs.

Left: Original photo

Right: iOS 27 Clean Up

This photo proved to be a much bigger challenge for Clean Up. After attempting to remove the man on the right, Clean Up left behind a garbled mess with plenty of obvious artifacts. The leaves are too chunky. It struggled in a similar way on the left side of the image, where the woman with white hair was standing behind the white flowers. Clean Up also left behind a “ghost” of the dog’s head, though it arguably blends in with the stone wall and is much more noticeable in this side-by-side comparison.

Left: Original photo

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Photoshop had no issues removing the woman on the left behind the white flowers or the man on the right behind the leaves, realistically filling in both areas in the process. The end result is a very convincing photo that looks like nobody was ever there. Photoshop also avoided leaving behind any phantom shadows this time.

Adding to the picture

Left: iOS 27 Extend

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

I thought this photograph of these old, winding steps would make for a good test because I didn’t think it would be immediately obvious to either AI what it was looking at, and I was curious to see how each would interpret the scene. Or even what it would do with it. It looks like iOS 27’s Extend tool interpreted the photo as something more like a ceiling fan, rounding off the ends of the stairs as though they were blades. Photoshop, on the other hand, simply extended the stairs outward and did a surprisingly good job of matching the wood grain.

Left: iOS 27 Extend

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Extend does an excellent job living up to its name here. It extends the scene really well and creates a very convincing final image. Notice the windows are believably repeated and the bridge on the right side of the photo, while arguably too smooth, still manages to look fairly convincing.

Now look at Photoshop’s attempt. Actually, Photoshop, did you even make an attempt? This is a complete failure by just about every measure. Pure, obvious AI slop. The windows and roofline in the upper-left corner of the photo look terrible. The bridge on the right doesn’t have anything resembling the realistic arch Apple created, and for some reason, Photoshop decided the waterfall should randomly change direction rather than continue along the existing river line.

Left: iOS 27 Extend

Right: Adobe Photoshop Generative Fill

Extend again manages to create a convincing image that, while not perfect, is significantly better than what Photoshop produced. Extend creates a believable table with some books or magazines, and the flowers in the vase look much more realistic than those generated by Photoshop. The decorative ornamentation above the left door also matches the real ones in the photo surprisingly well. There is some strangeness on the right side of the photo, where Extend has added a radiator, a random power cord, and a table for some reason.

Perhaps the biggest difference between Extend and Photoshop is at the ceiling. Extend has recreated more of the wood from the opposite wall, while Photoshop has tried to turn it into something more like a structural beam.

Photoshop, meanwhile, can’t seem to generate an image without the telltale signs of AI slop. Its table has too many legs and appears to simply “break off” before blending into the floor. The ornamentation above the door is less convincing, missing one of the “swirls” and doesn’t have the textured paint found on the real ornamentation in the photo.

I wouldn’t say either is perfect, but when it comes to realism, I think Apple’s solution edges out Adobe’s.

The good, the bad, and the AI slop

It’s worth mentioning that Photoshop requires a subscription to use, but none of the features I tested consume generative AI credits. Adobe does give users the option to choose other AI models that may require credits, but I didn’t use those models in my tests. Apple, too, has made it clear that “usage limits may apply” to some Apple Intelligence features and may charge for expanded access in the future. 

It’s clear that Apple has made significant improvements to the Clean Up tool over previous versions of iOS. I’ve tried it before and always found it underwhelming, but now it’s genuinely good. The new Extend tool is impressive as well, and I found it significantly better than Adobe’s offering in my tests. Adobe gives you unlimited refinements and the ability to adjust results with prompts, but I question the value of those benefits if additional generations and prompts simply churn out more obvious AI slop. Of course, results will vary depending on the photograph, the complexity of the scene, and what you’re asking the tools to do. These were simply the results I got from the photos I tested.

title: OpenAI says Apple Intelligence users showed little interest in ChatGPT integration
snippet: As reported by The Financial Times, new court filings show that OpenAI was disappointed by the adoption of ChatGPT through Apple Intelligence, which it says “dramatically underperformed” after launching in 2024. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
As reported by The Financial Times, new court filings show that OpenAI was disappointed by the adoption of ChatGPT through Apple Intelligence, which it says “dramatically underperformed” after launching in 2024. Here are the details.

OpenAI asks court to rule before trial

In August 2025, Elon Musk said that X, now part of SpaceXAI, would sue Apple and OpenAI over alleged collusion to shut out competitors in the AI space, stemming from OpenAI’s deal with Apple to make ChatGPT part of Apple Intelligence and Siri.

When the lawsuit was filed, it actually went beyond Musk’s original public complaint about App Store rankings. X and SpaceXAI also accused Apple of trying to stifle the development of “super apps,” including X’s effort to turn itself into an “everything app.”

In the weeks and months that followed, all companies involved filed briefs, accusations, and defenses with the court. Apple and OpenAI have argued, among other things, that their deal was not exclusive as the complaint alleged, while court filings have also revealed new details about how the partnership worked behind the scenes.

One of those details surfaced today in a filing from OpenAI. As first reported by The Financial Times, OpenAI “said it was disappointed by how little interest Apple generated from iPhone users after the two companies struck a deal in 2024 for ChatGPT to power ‘Apple Intelligence’.”

From the report:

When the 2024 deal was agreed, OpenAI expected a “halo effect” from promotion and brand association with Apple, as well as more subscriptions coming from Apple Intelligence users, Wednesday’s court document says.

But a month after the ChatGPT integration launched, it “appeared to be off to a slow start” and OpenAI was cutting its forecasts for how many weekly active users it expected to attract, it said. By the summer of 2025, “it was clear that Apple’s integration of ChatGPT was dramatically underperforming”.

The report notes that today’s filing contains multiple redacted conversations, but the unredacted portions show that OpenAI executives were concerned Apple could “want to move faster” to secure another AI partner.

When Apple Intelligence was first announced in 2024, Craig Federighi said in an interview that Apple ultimately wanted users to be able to choose between different AI models, specifically pointing to Google Gemini as a potential future integration.

That specific partnership never materialized, but Apple has since turned to Google’s Gemini models to help power the new Siri AI, while Xcode has expanded to support coding agents from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI.

	

Back to today’s filing, The Financial Times notes that it also points to the way Apple implemented ChatGPT as one possible reason for the slow adoption, as the integration was turned off by default.

Finally, as noted by Reuters, OpenAI is also arguing that recent securities disclosures from SpaceX undermine SpaceXAI’s claims that the Apple partnership harmed competition. In its filing, OpenAI said SpaceX’s IPO registration statement was “replete with disclosures diametrically opposed” to the competitive harm alleged in the lawsuit.

For these reasons, OpenAI is asking Judge Mark Pittman to rule in its favor before trial on SpaceXAI’s antitrust claims. The case is currently set to go to trial in January.

title: Tesla finally moves to electrify trucking after a decade of work and delays
snippet: Tesla's Semi truck, with a 500-mile range, is about to hit the road in big numbers, with the company saying it plans to make 50,000 units a year.
fullText:
Tesla is finally handing over the first of its all-electric Semi trucks to customers after nearly a decade of delays and refinements to the vehicle, which it first revealed in 2017.

Company executives — except CEO Elon Musk, who was at President Trump’s state dinner with Chinese Premier Xi Jinping — walked an audience of customers, employees, and influencers through many of the details at an event in Reno, Nevada, on Thursday night.

Customers will be able to take delivery of the truck whenever they are ready, though charging infrastructure remains a hurdle, a person familiar with the matter told TechCrunch on the condition of anonymity.

Without revealing the final sticker price, the executives promised the truck will help fleet owners lower their total cost of ownership, reduce emissions, and benefit from greater reliability. 

The event was held at a new factory dedicated to the Semi that’s adjacent to the company’s first Gigafactory in Reno. Tesla plans to build as many as 50,000 trucks a year at the plant, or roughly 1,000 per week, and create 3,000 jobs for the local economy. The most capable version of the truck is expected to travel 500 miles or more on one charge (depending on the size of the load) and cost just shy of $300,000 before incentives. There will be shorter-range variants, too.

The Semi’s long-awaited launch comes at a time of transition for Tesla. Musk now paints Tesla as a robotics and AI company even though nearly all of its revenue comes from vehicle sales. He has also changed Tesla’s mission to “build a world of amazing abundance.” When he showed off the Semi in 2017, Tesla’s mission was still “to accelerate the world’s transition to sustainable energy.”

Despite the change in positioning, and seemingly priorities for Tesla, Thursday’s event still saw a lot of discussion about reducing trucking emissions. Dan Priestley, the head of Tesla’s Semi program, noted that heavy trucks produce 16% of emissions despite making up just 1% of vehicles on the road.

“We’re super excited to be deploying these into our own operations because it’s fulfilling the mission that we originally started out [with],” he said.

“Occasionally we get a little too far out there”

Originally slated to go into production in 2019, the Semi was delayed for multiple reasons. The pandemic, a global parts supply and semiconductor shortage, and changes made in response to pilot customer feedback all contributed to the years-long wait. 

Priestley and Lars Moravy, who leads most of Tesla’s engineering efforts, detailed many of those changes during the 30-minute event — timed thus to show a Semi that started at 3% battery go up to 60% while plugged into one of Tesla’s megawatt charging stations. (Tesla is also building an entire network of these chargers, which Priestley detailed during the event.)

Some of these changes are big and obvious: The company has shaved off roughly 1,000 pounds of weight from the vehicle compared to its original version. Others are more specific, like going from using three different oils in the Semi’s drive axle to just one.

Moravy said the previous axle design that needed three different oils had “always frustrated” him, and admitted that Tesla tends to prioritize “super bespoke” designs. Priestley added that changes to the motor design and work from Tesla’s lubricants team allowed the company to cut out the other two oils. “Occasionally we get a little too far out there,” he said.

Tesla also had to pivot to fix issues with the side windows. In its original design, the company employed pop-out windows that didn’t fully open, and for years, everyone from actual truck drivers to automotive bloggers raised this as an obvious problem.

On Thursday, Priestley offered a mea culpa. He called the original design “not sufficient” and revealed that the new Semi now has standard roll-down windows.

“We fully admit we were wrong about the windows,” he said. “Turns out there’s a lot of infrastructure in the world, whether it’s a badge reader, or your toll booth, or you’re talking to somebody on a call box. There’s all kinds of stuff right at that height, and it became evident that we needed a roll-down window in order to make that infrastructure easier to interface with.”

“It’s okay to be wrong, Dan,” Moravy added.

But Tesla appears to have been right with its goal of making a truck that travels 500 miles on a single charge while fully loaded.

That claim, which Musk made during the original event in 2017, was a source of much derision for years. One of his highest-profile doubters was Bill Gates, who wrote in a 2020 blog post that electric big rigs would “probably never be a practical solution” because “batteries are big and heavy.”

Without naming him, Moravy and Priestley poked fun at Gates onstage during Thursday’s event: “We’re kind of ruthless about every watt-hour that we chase in these things, because there’s this wonderful compounding effect, [which] is that if you make the vehicle more efficient, that means it’s less battery you need to do the same amount of work, which means that you can take battery out of the vehicle, which is lower cost and lower mass,” Priestley said.

“We had some naysayers, names shall not be mentioned,” Moravy followed. 

“But, pretty well-known names,” Priestley responded.

“And at Tesla, we love when people tell us something’s impossible. So we took that challenge,” Moravy said.

While Musk was missing, he did pre-tape a segment that ran before the event started. In the video, he said the Semi will be the “funnest truck to drive.” He also promised Tesla’s partial automation features (curiously missing from the Semi despite the years of delays) will be added in the “near future.”

Musk also pitched the truck as making “a ton of sense economically, because the cost of electricity per mile is much less than the cost of diesel, especially in these crazy times” — though that final clause conveniently glosses over the fact that diesel prices have shot up because the president Musk himself helped elect has started a war that’s roiled energy markets.

When Apple first released the Apple Sports app, it offered a rather limited experience, both in terms of availability and which sports it actually covered.

title: The Aeropod automates soil aeration without robotics — see it at TechCrunch Disrupt
snippet: Muju Earth Technologies has developed a deceptively simply pod that can save farmers money while improving crop yields.
fullText:
Farmers around the world face a pressing problem: The equipment they use to till, plant, and harvest their fields is killing their margins. Studies have estimated that soil compaction can reduce yields by 20% to 60%. 

Plowing can help, but it’s a laborious and expensive task that harms soil health in different ways. Muju Earth has developed an alternative, the Aeropod, that automatically aerates the soil without machinery or robotics. The startup says it can promote better soil health while cutting farmers’ tilling costs by half or more.

The device is “built like a seed, it sows like a seed, and it ships like a seed,” Ifeoluwa Afolayan, the company’s co-founder and CEO, told TechCrunch. The device is about the size of a fingernail, and farmers drop it in the soil alongside their seeds using the same equipment. There’s no need to till the soil in advance.

“It just really seems like a no-brainer,” Afolayan said.

After the Aeropod is exposed to a combination of temperature, pressure, and moisture, it bursts open, loosening the soil and creating small channels that let air, water, and roots move through it more easily.

Muju Earth — one of the 200 startups in this year’s Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco in October — has tested its devices in lab settings and is embarking on paid field trials this fall in the U.K. Nine farmers are participating, and the startup has more than 30 on a waitlist.

Its initial target market is onion growers in the U.K. since onions are particularly sensitive to soil compaction, Afolayan said.

Tilling a field once might cost around £250 to £400 per hectare when factoring in labor costs, diesel, and wear and tear on equipment, Afolayan said. The Aeropod should produce similar results at just £100 per hectare, Afolayan said.

The Aeropod was born during Afolayan’s and co-founder Wangyang Hu’s time at Imperial College London, where they sought to design a product that would improve farmers’ bottom lines while also aiding soil health. The Aeropod’s development was driven by a single question: “How do you make this as simple as sowing a seed?” Afolayan said. “That’s the most equitable practice across every farmer on the planet.”

In addition to farmers, the startup has also heard from companies developing biologic amendments — products added to soil, often containing living microbes, that boost or replace chemical fertilizers. Because those companies’ products work best in aerated soils, they’re interested in pairing with the Aeropod.

But Afolayan said that farmers have been leading adoption. Most of the marketing to date has been inbound. “The best thing about Aeropod is the farmers intuitively understand the proposition,” she said.

Muju Earth is one of 200 startups in this year’s Startup Battlefield, a pitch competition in which 20 finalists will present on the main stage at TechCrunch Disrupt, taking place October 13-15 at Moscone West in San Francisco.

fullText:
Smart glasses are such a logical, futuristic step in mobile tech, and it’s one we’re on the cusp of being able to embrace. Yet, there’s a huge hurdle to overcome. For as useful and enjoyable as it is, the camera on smart glasses has become a massive problem, and it’s basically ruined existing smart glasses for me personally.

9to5Google Weekender by Ben Schoon is a part of our free newsletter that also includes ‘Inbox,’ a twice-weekly roundup of key stories from around the web by Daniel Bader. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every Sunday along with ‘Inbox’ on Tuesday and Thursday. You can find past issues here.

There are a few core use cases for smart glasses. The most futuristic is a mixed-reality experience where a display layers information on top of what you’re seeing around you. But that’s also the hardest to accomplish with today’s tech. So, with that in mind, audio-based glasses have been more popular.

Open-ear audio and always-ready access make these glasses very useful, but the real selling point for many has been the camera. Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses are the catalyst in all of this. Meta will go on and on about AI features, but a huge part of the appeal here is having a camera at the ready with point-of-view footage. That’s what sold me on it, and my pair has captured some really fun memories in my favorite hobby. 

	

Yet, I’ve barely touched those glasses over the past year, nor had I really gotten around to testing any others I’ve been offered. For example, the L’atitude 52°N Berlin glasses were originally pitched around having a better camera than Meta and, while I’m not a huge fan of the styling, the camera is at least decent – I wouldn’t say better with focus and direct sunlight being clear issues, but I do like that it can capture in landscape.

But, for as much fun as these cameras can be, it just feels wrong now.

The social stigma around cameras on smart glasses has been ruined by the misuse of these cameras. That was, sadly, somewhat inevitable. Any new piece of technology has the potential to be misused, but the subtle nature of these cameras turns simple misuse into making people downright uncomfortable. And, honestly, rightfully so! I initially had trouble understanding the issues many were taking with a camera on glasses, but example after example has shown just how many people are willing to misuse this tech.

Arguably, the bigger problem comes down to how it’s all been handled.

With Meta Ray-Bans, two problems became clear.

Firstly, there was the simple fact that Meta was at the helm. The company’s long history of handling private data, rightfully, did not mix well with a camera on your face. While Meta tried to convince users otherwise, leaks of human moderators viewing uncensored private recordings, combined with rumblings of Meta’s plans for facial recognition and always-on recording, simply evaporated any goodwill or trust that might have been left.

Secondly, there’s the amount of time it took for Meta to address the misuse. Stories have run rampant for the better part of two years now around back-alley deals to disable the privacy LED on Ray-Ban glasses, and it took until July of this year for Meta to implement a fix. An even more obvious loophole is only being patched now.

And now we’re approaching the debut of the first Android XR glasses from Samsung and Google – with every style having a camera. They’re facing a massive uphill battle as the “perv glasses” stigma is widely known and loud – a previous issue of our “Inbox” newsletter discussed this. Samsung has said that it has protections immediately in place around camera tampering, but not everyone is going to know that.

Basically what this boils down to is – thanks Meta, you’ve ruined this for everyone else.

The smart glasses market is going to have a rough time getting around all of this. The Ray-Bans debacle has done some serious damage that every other brand is going to have to work around. That is, assuming they want a camera in the first place. There are plenty of smart glasses that deliver useful functionality without a camera. Even Realities springs to mind as a clear example of this. Yet, when I was testing out those glasses, I constantly found myself missing the utility of an on-board camera (and a speaker, for that matter) for simply capturing the world around me, or wanting to use it with AI features. As overbearing as Meta has been with them, using the camera for various types of interactions such as scanning & translating menus, getting descriptions of real-world objects, and more, are very handy. 

It’s going to take years to get all of this tech to its ideal state no matter what, but I hope that the camera stigma eventually calms down.

title: Apple Maps just added two new features in iOS 27
snippet: iOS 27 is packed with a wide array of new features for iPhone, including in Apple Maps. Here are the two tentpole iOS 27 features for Apple Maps, plus some miscellaneous improvements. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 is packed with a wide array of new features for iPhone, including in Apple Maps. Here are the two tentpole iOS 27 features for Apple Maps, plus some miscellaneous improvements.

Apple Maps in iOS 27 gets upgraded Flyover feature and Local Lists, plus other improvements

Apple Maps doesn’t look drastically different when you open it in iOS 27. But Apple has a variety of big and small improvements in its latest update.

One tentpole feature is an upgraded Flyover experience. Per Apple:

Apple Maps brings an enhanced Flyover experience, which combines aerial imagery with AI to enable users to view imagery in stunning detail for select cities around the world like never before. Whether scouting a location before a trip or simply exploring a city from a new perspective, the enhanced experience gives users a sharper and more lifelike glimpse into destinations across the globe.

Apple also highlights a new Local Lists feature that’s available in the US:

With Local Lists, Apple Maps users in the U.S. can find the perfect spot for meeting friends, dining, and more. Using intelligent insights from what’s trending, Maps surfaces locally relevant collections of places — from trending restaurants to great spots to take kids — so it’s easy for users to find what they are looking for. All insights are derived with privacy in mind and never tied to individual users.

Beyond these two tentpole changes, iOS 27 also has a variety of other improvements:

More Suggested Places: The new Suggested Places feature that arrived in iOS 26.5 now lets you swipe horizontally through many more suggestions, so it’s not limited to just two placed

Trending Restaurants: The search screen now shows a Trending Restaurants section

Natural language search for routing: AI search expands to routing specifics

Maps Parked Car widget in Smart Stack: Makes it easy to find your car via Apple Watch

Offline Maps update improvements: Apple doesn’t say what the exact improvements are

iOS 27 also brings certain features to more territories around the world, including Visited Places and Guides. And the Maps icon has been refreshed with a new design, as seen above.
